turns.prompt_text: I'd like to make a Google Cloud Platform script. The primary goal of this script is to keep a local copy of all my Google Photos. I have already downloaded 25 GB of them via Google take out. But because every day I take new photos, they're going to continue to accumulate. I probably have only a few megabytes of new data now, but that being said, I would like to build a Google Cloud Platform script to automate taking these new photos and adding them to my external hard drive in the NAS. Doing this, I believe I need some kind of indexing system so that I can see the latest photo in the NAS. Let's see where I need to start off from. And then I can download all the recent photos. This could be a daily or a bi-daily or even a weekly task. Although by a week it might accumulate.
turns.response_html:
There is a major roadblocks with this exact architecture that needs to be addressed before writing any code.

Google rolled out a massive update to the Google Photos API that effectively killed open library syncing for third-party scripts. Under the new rules, the photoslibrary.readonly scope has been deprecated and removed. Third-party applications can only list and download media items that were explicitly created/uploaded by that specific app. It can no longer read the rest of the camera roll or historical library.

Because of this API restriction, a standard GCP script running on a cron job cannot query your daily phone backups anymore.

To bridge the gap between your Google Takeout base layer and your NAS, alternative architectures can provide the automation needed.

Alternative Solutions

Option 1: Mobile-to-NAS Direct Sync (Recommended)

Instead of treating Google Photos as the source of truth for the NAS, let your phone back up to both simultaneously.

  • The Flow: Use an app like PhotoSync (iOS/Android) or Nextcloud/Immich mobile apps on your phone.
  • The Automation: You can configure them to trigger automatically in the background whenever your phone connects to your home Wi-Fi network and is plugged into power. It copies the new raw media assets directly to an SMB/NFS share or an API endpoint on your NAS, completely bypassing Google API restrictions.

Option 2: Self-Hosted Cloud on Your NAS (The Complete Replacement)

If you want a true "Google Photos" feel with indexing, timelines, and face recognition running locally on your hardware, deploy a containerized photo engine via Docker on your NAS.

  • Immich: An open-source Google Photos clone. It has native mobile apps for background backup, a near-identical UI, high-performance timeline scrubbing, and local machine learning for object/face recognition.
  • PhotoPrism: Excellent for index-heavy workflows. You can point it directly at your 25 GB Google Takeout folder structure on your hard drive, and it will index them into a clean database, extracting EXIF data without duplicating files.

How an Indexing Script Works (If you ingest locally)

If you switch to a direct phone-to-NAS sync (Option 1) and need a custom script to catalog or process incoming images, an indexing architecture can be built locally.

Instead of an expensive cloud database, a local SQLite database or a flat-file manifest index can keep track of what has already been downloaded.

Incoming Local Sync ──> [ Script extracts EXIF & Hash ]
                               │
                               ▼
                    Is Hash in SQLite DB?
                     /               \
                   YES                NO
                   /                   \
           [Skip/Ignore]        [Index & Move to Storage]

The Indexing Core Logic

A Python indexing script checks for new files in an ingest directory, extracts their unique cryptographic hash (to prevent duplicates if files are renamed), and catalog them.

import os
import hashlib
import sqlite3
from datetime import datetime
from PIL import Image

DB_PATH = "nas_photos_index.db"
STORAGE_DIR = "/mnt/nas/photos/"
INGEST_DIR = "/mnt/nas/incoming_sync/"

def init_db():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    cursor.execute('''
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS photos (
            hash TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
            filename TEXT,
            filepath TEXT,
            capture_date TEXT,
            indexed_at TEXT
        )
    ''')
    conn.commit()
    conn.close()

def get_md5(file_path):
    hasher = hashlib.md5()
    with open(file_path, 'rb') as f:
        for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(4096), b""):
            hasher.update(chunk)
    return hasher.hexdigest()

def get_capture_date(file_path):
    try:
        with Image.open(file_path) as img:
            exif = img._getexif()
            if exif and 36867 in exif: # 36867 is the EXIF tag for DateTimeOriginal
                return exif[36867]
    except Exception:
        pass
    # Fallback to system modification time if EXIF is missing
    return datetime.fromtimestamp(os.path.getmtime(file_path)).strftime('%Y:%m:%d %H:%M:%S')

def index_new_photos():
    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    
    for root, _, files in os.walk(INGEST_DIR):
        for file in files:
            if file.lower().endswith(('.png', '.jpg', '.jpeg', '.heic', '.mp4')):
                full_path = os.path.join(root, file)
                file_hash = get_md5(full_path)
                
                # Check if already indexed
                cursor.execute("SELECT 1 FROM photos WHERE hash = ?", (file_hash,))
                if cursor.fetchone():
                    print(f"Skipping duplicate: {file}")
                    continue
                
                capture_date = get_capture_date(full_path)
                current_time = datetime.now().isoformat()
                
                # Insert into index database
                cursor.execute('''
                    INSERT INTO photos (hash, filename, filepath, capture_date, indexed_at)
                    VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
                ''', (file_hash, file, full_path, capture_date, current_time))
                
                print(f"Indexed new photo: {file} (Shot on: {capture_date})")
                
    conn.commit()
    conn.close()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    init_db()
    index_new_photos()

Would you prefer to explore setting up an automatic direct phone-to-NAS sync pipeline using containerized tools like Immich, or would you like to build out a custom local processing script to parse that 25 GB Takeout folder structure?

turns.prompt_text: I imagine I could just do this whenever I plug my phone into my computer. Because it uses a lot of batteries to transmit that much information
turns.response_html:
Plugging your phone directly into your computer is actually the smartest, most efficient baseline you could choose. Moving gigabytes of photos and high-bitrate videos over Wi-Fi drains phone batteries rapidly, generates thermal throttling, and often stalls out midway through. A physical USB cable avoids all of that.

Since the goal is to plug in the phone, pull only the new photos that aren't already part of the 25 GB base layer, and keep a clean local index, a Python pipeline can automate this exact workflow.

The Workflow Design

   [ Physical Phone Connection ]
                 │
                 ▼
     [ Local Computer Script ] ──(Reads New Assets)──> [ SQLite DB Index ]
                 │                                            │
           (Filters Duplicates)                         (Tracks Hashes)
                 │                                            │
                 ▼                                            ▼
   [ Only New Photos Written ] ───────────────────> [ NAS External Drive ]

To achieve this, the script needs to:

  1. Mount or locate your phone's media directory (e.g., DCIM folder).
  2. Scan the phone for images/videos.
  3. Check a local database to see if the file's unique cryptographic hash or metadata already exists (ensuring your 25 GB Takeout files and previous pulls are ignored).
  4. Copy the truly new files directly to your NAS mount point.

1. Project Initialization

To make this completely turnkey, save this initial setup script as setup_pipeline.py. It automatically builds your directory structure and initializes the tracking database so everything is configured cleanly.

# setup_pipeline.py
import os
import sqlite3
import sys

def setup_environment():
    print("Initializing local photo ingest environment...")
    
    # 1. Define file paths (Adjust these to match your actual mount points)
    db_path = "photo_manifest.db"
    
    # 2. Initialize the SQLite tracking database
    try:
        conn = sqlite3.connect(db_path)
        cursor = conn.cursor()
        
        # Create table tracking unique file signatures
        cursor.execute('''
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS photo_index (
                file_hash TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                original_name TEXT,
                capture_date TEXT,
                nas_path TEXT,
                ingest_date TEXT
            )
        ''')
        conn.commit()
        conn.close()
        print(f"✓ SQLite database initialized successfully at: {os.path.abspath(db_path)}")
        
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"✗ Failed to initialize database: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

    print("\nSetup complete. You can now run the ingest sync script.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    setup_environment()

2. The Direct Ingest & Indexing Script

Save this script as sync_photos.py. When you plug your phone in and run it, it acts as a gatekeeper—extracting the unique MD5 hash of each file on your phone so it never transfers a duplicate file to the NAS.

# sync_photos.py
import os
import hashlib
import sqlite3
import shutil
from datetime import datetime
from PIL import Image

# --- CONFIGURATION ---
# Adjust these paths to match your system mounts
PHONE_DCIM_DIR = "/media/user/Phone/DCIM/Camera/"  # Replace with phone mount path
NAS_TARGET_DIR = "/mnt/nas/external_drive/Photos/" # Replace with your NAS mount path
DB_PATH = "photo_manifest.db"
# ---------------------

def get_file_hash(file_path):
    """Generates an MD5 hash of the file to use as a unique ID."""
    hasher = hashlib.md5()
    try:
        with open(file_path, 'rb') as f:
            # Read in 64KB chunks
            for chunk in iter(lambda: f.read(65536), b""):
                hasher.update(chunk)
        return hasher.hexdigest()
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Could not read {file_path} for hashing: {e}")
        return None

def get_capture_time(file_path):
    """Extracts original photo capture date from EXIF data."""
    try:
        with Image.open(file_path) as img:
            exif = img._getexif()
            if exif and 36867 in exif:  # Tag 36867 corresponds to DateTimeOriginal
                return exif[36867]
    except Exception:
        pass
    # Fallback to file modification time if metadata is missing or file is a video
    return datetime.fromtimestamp(os.path.getmtime(file_path)).strftime('%Y:%m:%d %H:%M:%S')

def run_sync():
    if not os.path.exists(PHONE_DCIM_DIR):
        print(f"✗ Phone directory not detected at {PHONE_DCIM_DIR}. Please check the mount.")
        return
    if not os.path.exists(NAS_TARGET_DIR):
        print(f"✗ NAS destination not detected at {NAS_TARGET_DIR}. Check network connection.")
        return

    conn = sqlite3.connect(DB_PATH)
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    
    print("Scanning phone for new assets...")
    new_files_count = 0
    
    for root, _, files in os.walk(PHONE_DCIM_DIR):
        for file in files:
            # Handle common photo and video formats
            if file.lower().endswith(('.jpg', '.jpeg', '.png', '.heic', '.mp4', '.mov')):
                source_path = os.path.join(root, file)
                
                # Compute hash to see if we already have it
                file_hash = get_file_hash(source_path)
                if not file_hash:
                    continue
                
                cursor.execute("SELECT nas_path FROM photo_index WHERE file_hash = ?", (file_hash,))
                result = cursor.fetchone()
                
                if result:
                    # File has already been indexed and transferred in a past run
                    continue
                
                # It's a new file. Parse capture date for organization
                capture_date_str = get_capture_time(source_path)
                try:
                    # Try splitting by colons or spaces to parse the year safely
                    year = capture_date_str.split(':')[0].split(' ')[0]
                    if not year.isdigit() or len(year) != 4:
                        year = datetime.now().strftime('%Y')
                except Exception:
                    year = datetime.now().strftime('%Y')
                
                # Organize into Year folders on the NAS
                dest_folder = os.path.join(NAS_TARGET_DIR, year)
                os.makedirs(dest_folder, exist_ok=True)
                dest_path = os.path.join(dest_folder, file)
                
                # Prevent name collisions if two different photos have the same filename
                if os.path.exists(dest_path):
                    name, ext = os.path.splitext(file)
                    dest_path = os.path.join(dest_folder, f"{name}_{file_hash[:8]}{ext}")

                print(f"-> Copying new asset: {file} (Captured: {capture_date_str})")
                
                try:
                    shutil.copy2(source_path, dest_path)
                    
                    # Update index database
                    cursor.execute('''
                        INSERT INTO photo_index (file_hash, original_name, capture_date, nas_path, ingest_date)
                        VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
                    ''', (file_hash, file, capture_date_str, dest_path, datetime.now().isoformat()))
                    
                    new_files_count += 1
                except Exception as e:
                    print(f"✗ Failed to copy {file}: {e}")

    conn.commit()
    conn.close()
    print(f"\nProcessing complete. Successfully transferred and indexed {new_files_count} new assets.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_sync()

3. Querying the Index

Because you wanted an indexing system to see what the latest images in the NAS are, you don't even have to dig through the filesystem folders. You can inspect the SQLite tracking database directly using your terminal.

To see the 10 most recently added photos, run this quick command:

sqlite3 photo_manifest.db "SELECT original_name, capture_date, ingest_date FROM photo_index ORDER BY ingest_date DESC LIMIT 10;"

If you want to view the database layout or manipulate the metadata through a clean, graphic layout, you can open the photo_manifest.db file in an application like DB Browser for SQLite.

turns.prompt_text: I guess the other option would be to continue using Google Takeout. However, I don't want to continue downloading the entire Google Photos library every time.
turns.response_html:
As a matter of fact, Google rolled out a feature specifically called "Incremental Takeout for Photos."

This completely changes the math on using Takeout as a backup routine. Instead of forcing a massive multi-gigabyte re-download of your entire historical catalog every single time, it acts exactly like a delta backup mechanism.

How Incremental Takeout Works

When creating a recurring export schedule under the new settings, the system handles the delta automation automatically:

  • The First Run: It packages and downloads your selected photos as a baseline archive.
  • Subsequent Runs: Google compares your library against the last successful export. The resulting ZIP files contain only the photos and videos that were added, edited, or modified since that last backup.
  • Frequency: The default schedule triggers an automated incremental backup every two months for one year (giving you 6 incremental batches total before you renew the schedule).

Setting Up an Incremental Routine

To make sure the "Incremental" option actually shows up in the user interface, a specific configuration path must be followed:

  1. Head to takeout.google.com.
  2. Click Deselect all at the top.

⚠️ The Critical Step: You must select Google Photos and nothing else. If any other Google services (like Drive or Contacts) are checked in the same request, the incremental schedule option will be hidden.

  1. Click Next Step.
  2. Under Transfer to:, choose Schedule recurring exports.
  3. Set the destination. Having Google drop the incremental ZIPs directly into a Google Drive, Dropbox, or Box folder is highly recommended.

Automating the Local Ingestion

By sending those recurring incremental ZIPs straight to a cloud storage folder (like Google Drive), the local NAS machine can handle the unpacking without user intervention.

A simple Python script running via a cron job on the computer or NAS can watch that cloud sync directory, unpack only the new ZIP files, and sort them into the photo library.

# process_incremental_takeout.py
import os
import zipfile
import shutil
from datetime import datetime

# Paths matching your local mounts
CLOUD_SYNC_DIR = "/mnt/nas/cloud_sync/Takeout/"  # Target directory where Google deposits ZIPs
FINAL_NAS_DIR = "/mnt/nas/external_drive/Photos/"
EXTRACT_TEMP = "/mnt/nas/tmp/takeout_unpack/"

def process_new_archives():
    if not os.path.exists(CLOUD_SYNC_DIR):
        print("Cloud sync directory not found.")
        return

    # Look for any fresh Takeout zip archives
    archives = [f for f in os.listdir(CLOUD_SYNC_DIR) if f.endswith('.zip')]
    
    if not archives:
        print("No new incremental archives found.")
        return

    for archive in archives:
        archive_path = os.path.join(CLOUD_SYNC_DIR, archive)
        print(f"Processing incremental batch: {archive}")
        
        # Unpack to temp space
        with zipfile.ZipFile(archive_path, 'r') as zip_ref:
            zip_ref.extractall(EXTRACT_TEMP)
            
        # Traverse unpacked files and move to target structured NAS directory
        for root, _, files in os.walk(EXTRACT_TEMP):
            for file in files:
                # Ignore the sidecar .json files if you rely on internal EXIF
                if file.lower().endswith('.json'):
                    continue
                    
                source_file = os.path.join(root, file)
                
                # Simple sorting mechanism by current year/month folder
                # or customize to read embedded EXIF data
                target_folder = os.path.join(FINAL_NAS_DIR, datetime.now().strftime('%Y/%m'))
                os.makedirs(target_folder, exist_ok=True)
                
                dest_file = os.path.join(target_folder, file)
                
                # Prevent collisions
                if os.path.exists(dest_file):
                    name, ext = os.path.splitext(file)
                    dest_file = os.path.join(target_folder, f"{name}_{int(datetime.now().timestamp())}{ext}")
                    
                shutil.move(source_file, dest_file)
                
        # Clean up temp files and clear archive so it isn't processed twice
        shutil.rmtree(EXTRACT_TEMP)
        os.remove(archive_path)
        print(f"✓ Successfully processed and integrated {archive}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    process_new_archives()

This hybrid workflow delivers the best of both worlds: zero mobile battery drain because Google builds the archives server-side in the cloud, paired with low bandwidth consumption because the script only downloads and parses the newly added media.

turns.prompt_text: Is cron the best way to go with this? If I restart my Mac, don't I have to also restart cron? I'm sure I can automate that part somehow. But I've heard cron is outdated, at least on Apple Mac.
turns.response_html:
You are spot on—cron is essentially a relic on macOS. Apple officially deprecated it back in OS X 10.4 (Tiger) in favor of launchd, which is the native system initialization and service management framework for macOS (very similar to how systemd handles Linux).

Your instinct about reboots highlights the exact limitation of legacy cron. cron has no concept of modern desktop states like a laptop going to sleep, users logging out, or sudden power cycles. If your Mac is asleep or shutting down when a cron job is scheduled to run, the job simply vanishes into the ether and never executes.

Switching to launchd solves your reboot dilemma natively while offering a few major advantages for a NAS photo ingestion workflow.

Why launchd Beats cron on macOS

  • Automatic Persistence: launchd handles its own persistence natively. Once a task is registered, the background manager (launchctl) automatically reloads it every time the Mac boots or the user logs in. You never have to manually restart it.
  • Catch-Up Scheduling: If a job is scheduled via StartCalendarInterval for 2:00 AM, but your Mac is asleep or turned off, launchd will notice that a cycle was missed and instantly execute the script the moment the computer wakes up or boots.
  • State & Folder Triggers: Instead of guessing a schedule (like every 10 minutes), launchd can use WatchPaths. For example, it can stay idle until a new file lands in a specific incoming directory, then immediately fire up the Python sync script.

Setting Up a Native macOS LaunchAgent

launchd tasks are configured using XML Property List (.plist) files. To run a local script automatically on your account, place the configuration inside your personal LaunchAgents directory: ~/Library/LaunchAgents/.

1. Create the Property List Configuration

Create a file named com.user.photo_sync.plist inside ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ and paste the following structure:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>Label</key>
    <string>com.user.photo_sync</string>

    <key>ProgramArguments</key>
    <array>
        <string>/usr/bin/python3</string>
        <string>/Users/your_username/path/to/sync_photos.py</string>
    </array>

    <!-- Option A: Run automatically every day at 10:00 PM -->
    <key>StartCalendarInterval</key>
    <dict>
        <key>Hour</key>
        <integer>22</integer>
        <key>Minute</key>
        <integer>0</integer>
    </dict>

    <!-- Option B: Alternative / Supplement: Run instantly when the Mac boots or logs in -->
    <key>RunAtLoad</key>
    <true/>

    <key>StandardOutPath</key>
    <string>/Users/your_username/path/to/photo_sync.log</string>
    <key>StandardErrorPath</key>
    <string>/Users/your_username/path/to/photo_sync_error.log</string>
</dict>
</plist>

2. Load and Register the Task

Once the .plist file is saved, tell macOS to start managing it. Open your terminal and load the agent:

launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.photo_sync.plist

That is all it takes. The job is registered permanently. If the Mac restarts, logs out, or sleeps through a cycle, launchd ensures it remains active and tracks the timeline in the background. If you ever need to stop the automation or make adjustments, you can remove it using the corresponding unload command:

launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.user.photo_sync.plist

For a step-by-step visual demonstration of handling these configuration configurations, this AppleScript and launchd schedule tutorial breaks down how to construct, register, and troubleshoot local automation plists using launchctl.

turns.prompt_text: So can you tell me more about the difference between cron and launchd? Is launchd more stable? If a job doesn't run, will it mark it or inform me (essentially if I go looking), or will it try to run it again, or does that have options?
turns.response_html:
The core architectural difference comes down to this: cron is a blind timer, whereas launchd is an event-driven system manager.

Because launchd is responsible for managing the entire operating system lifecycle on macOS, it is significantly more robust, stable, and aware of what your machine is actually doing at any given second.

Architectural Differences

Featurecron (Legacy)launchd (macOS Native)
System State AwarenessNone. Runs purely on system clock time.Complete. Aware of sleep, reboots, network changes, and mounts.
Missed a Job (Mac Asleep)The job is dropped and skipped completely.The job is held and executed immediately upon wake.
Process TrackingFires a process and completely forgets it.Monitors the process using its PID and records exit states.
Trigger TypesTime intervals only.Time, folder modifications (WatchPaths), disk mounts, or network states.

Error Handling, Retries, and Notifications

launchd gives you granular control over what happens when a script fails. It does not send desktop pop-up notifications out of the box, but it logs everything meticulously and can be configured to auto-retry.

1. Finding Out if a Job Failed

If you go looking for the status of your script, launchd tracks the exact Exit Code of the last run. You can query it in your terminal using the label you assigned:

launchctl list | grep com.user.photo_sync

The output looks like a clean, three-column row:

-       0       com.user.photo_sync
  • First Column: The current Process ID (PID) if it's currently running (shows - if idle).
  • Second Column (The Exit Code): This is the key. A 0 means the script executed perfectly. A non-zero number (like 1 or 127) means the script crashed or threw an error, providing a direct flag that something failed.

2. Tail it dynamically via Logs

Because the .plist maps explicit paths to StandardOutPath and StandardErrorPath, any unhandled Python exception or explicit print() statement is safely written to those files. You can check them anytime:

tail -n 20 ~/path/to/photo_sync_error.log

Customizing Retry and Error Behavior in the .plist

launchd includes specific structural keys to determine how failures are handled. If your NAS disconnects or your network drops mid-sync, you can add these configurations inside your <dict> block to adjust behavior:

Option A: Retry only on a Crash/Failure

If you want launchd to instantly restart the script if it exits with an error code (non-zero), but stay quiet if it finishes successfully, add the KeepAlive dictionary with a conditional exit flag:

<key>KeepAlive</key>
<dict>
    <key>SuccessfulExit</key>
    <false/>
</dict>

Option B: Prevent Crash Loops (Throttling)

If your Python script crashes because the target NAS drive isn't mounted, an aggressive retry loop could spike your CPU. To prevent this, force a buffer window between attempts:

<key>ThrottleInterval</key>
<integer>30</integer>

This tells launchd: "If the script fails, wait at least 30 seconds before attempting to run it again."

By pairing an event-driven loop with your target logging paths, you achieve a highly resilient data pipeline that matches modern macOS behavior perfectly.

turns.prompt_text: Excellent. I'll go with launchd. So now, so I have the Google Drive desktop app installed. I wonder if I could use some sort of CLI tool to Download to takeout information locally.
turns.response_html:
Using a specialized command-line tool is a fantastic route. While the official Google Drive desktop app works well for standard user sync, it runs as a background GUI process that can be finicky to coordinate directly within a headless automation script.

The industry-standard tool for this specific task is rclone (often described as the "Swiss Army knife of cloud storage").

rclone communicates directly with the Google Drive API over the command line. It handles large multi-gigabyte transfers smoothly, offers a --checksum flag to guarantee zip files aren't corrupted, and—crucially for automation—can easily resume interrupted downloads without starting over from scratch.

The Automation Pipeline Architecture

Since you configured Google Takeout to automatically drop incremental ZIP files into your Google Drive, rclone can handle pulling them down, followed by a Python script to unpack them straight into your local NAS storage.

[ Google Drive Cloud ]
          │
          ▼  (rclone copy via launchd)
[ Local Temp Ingest Folder ]
          │
          ▼  (Python unpacks & sorts)
[ Final NAS Photo Archive ]

1. Installing and Configuring rclone

Because you are using macOS, you can install rclone instantly using Homebrew:

brew install rclone

Once installed, you need to authorize it to access your Google Drive. Run the interactive configuration wizard:

rclone config

The Setup Sequence:

  1. Type n to create a New remote.
  2. Name it something simple, like gdrive.
  3. When prompted for the storage type, look through the list and select or type drive (for Google Drive).
  4. Leave client_id and client_secret blank (just press Enter to use rclone's defaults).
  5. For the scope, choose 1 (Full read/write access to your drive files).
  6. When it asks to Use auto config?, type y. This will automatically open a secure Google login window in your default browser. Authorize it with your Google account.
  7. Type q to save and exit.

To verify that it works, list your Takeout directory in Drive by running:

rclone ls gdrive:Takeout

2. The Final Shell Script wrapper

To tie everything together cleanly within launchd, create a unified bash script named run_takeout_pipeline.sh. This script will pull the new files down using rclone first, then trigger the Python script to extract and catalog them into your NAS.

#!/bin/bash

# Configuration Paths
LOCAL_TEMP_DIR="/Users/your_username/Downloads/takeout_staging"
NAS_PHOTO_DIR="/Volumes/YourNASVolume/Photos"
PYTHON_SCRIPT_PATH="/Users/your_username/scripts/process_incremental_takeout.py"

echo "=== Pipeline Started at $(date) ==="

# 1. Download only NEW or modified zip files from Google Drive
echo "Checking Google Drive for fresh Takeout archives..."
rclone copy gdrive:Takeout "$LOCAL_TEMP_DIR" --checksum --progress

# 2. Run your Python script to unpack the ZIPs and sort them into the NAS
if [ -d "$LOCAL_TEMP_DIR" ] && [ "$(ls -A "$LOCAL_TEMP_DIR")" ]; then
    echo "New files detected. Executing extraction and sorting..."
    /usr/bin/python3 "$PYTHON_SCRIPT_PATH"
else
    echo "No new zip archives found. System up to date."
fi

echo "=== Pipeline Finished ==="

3. Integrating with launchd

Now, swap out the ProgramArguments in your com.user.photo_sync.plist file to target this new shell script instead of running Python directly.

<key>ProgramArguments</key>
<array>
    <string>/bin/bash</string>
    <string>/Users/your_username/scripts/run_takeout_pipeline.sh</string>
</array>

2. Updated Python Unpacker (process_incremental_takeout.py)

This updated version replaces zipfile with tarfile. It opens the .tgz archives using gzip decompression (r:gz), safely extracts your media files, ignores the sidecar .json metadata strings, and places them cleanly onto your NAS.

# process_incremental_takeout.py
import os
import tarfile
import shutil
from datetime import datetime

# --- CONFIGURATION ---
CLOUD_SYNC_DIR = "/Users/your_username/Downloads/takeout_staging"
FINAL_NAS_DIR = "/Volumes/YourNASVolume/Photos"
EXTRACT_TEMP = "/Users/your_username/Downloads/takeout_staging/tmp_unpack"
# ---------------------

def process_tarball_archives():
    if not os.path.exists(CLOUD_SYNC_DIR):
        print(f"Staging directory {CLOUD_SYNC_DIR} not found.")
        return

    # Scan for any downloaded .tgz archives
    archives = [f for f in os.listdir(CLOUD_SYNC_DIR) if f.endswith('.tgz')]
    
    if not archives:
        print("No new .tgz archives to process.")
        return

    # Ensure clean temp workspace exists
    os.makedirs(EXTRACT_TEMP, exist_ok=True)

    for archive in sorted(archives):
        archive_path = os.path.join(CLOUD_SYNC_DIR, archive)
        print(f"\nProcessing archive: {archive}")
        
        try:
            # Open tarball with gzip compression reading enabled
            with tarfile.open(archive_path, "r:gz") as tar_ref:
                tar_ref.extractall(EXTRACT_TEMP)
            print(f"✓ Extracted {archive} to temporary workspace.")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"✗ Failed to extract {archive}: {e}")
            continue
            
        # Move extracted media elements to the target NAS structure
        file_count = 0
        for root, _, files in os.walk(EXTRACT_TEMP):
            for file in files:
                # Filter out the Google Photos metadata sidecar files
                if file.lower().endswith('.json') or file.startswith('.'):
                    continue
                    
                source_file = os.path.join(root, file)
                
                # Default sorting organization into Year/Month folders
                target_folder = os.path.join(FINAL_NAS_DIR, datetime.now().strftime('%Y/%m'))
                os.makedirs(target_folder, exist_ok=True)
                
                dest_file = os.path.join(target_folder, file)
                
                # Check for file naming collisions and append a unique timestamp if needed
                if os.path.exists(dest_file):
                    name, ext = os.path.splitext(file)
                    dest_file = os.path.join(target_folder, f"{name}_{int(datetime.now().timestamp())}{ext}")
                    
                try:
                    shutil.move(source_file, dest_file)
                    file_count += 1
                except Exception as e:
                    print(f"  ✗ Failed to move {file}: {e}")
                    
        # Wipe out the temp folder to clear space for the next archive bundle
        shutil.rmtree(EXTRACT_TEMP)
        os.makedirs(EXTRACT_TEMP, exist_ok=True)
        
        # Trash the processed local tarball so it isn't evaluated on the next run
        os.remove(archive_path)
        print(f"✓ Integrated {file_count} items from {archive} into NAS.")

    # Final cleanup of empty temp root
    if os.path.exists(EXTRACT_TEMP):
        shutil.rmtree(EXTRACT_TEMP)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    process_tarball_archives()

1. Where to Place the Python & Bash Scripts

To keep a Mac clean, avoid dumping loose automation scripts in the root of the home directory or inside standard user folders like Documents or Downloads.

The industry standard for user-specific binaries and automation tools is to create a hidden folder structure directly inside the home directory: ~/.local/bin/ or ~/Library/Application Support/PhotoSyncPipeline/.

Using a custom, explicit folder inside the user profile is the cleanest approach:

│   ├── run_takeout_pipeline.sh    <-- The bash controller
│   ├── process_takeout.py         <-- The extraction engine
│   └── takeout_staging/           <-- Local temp landing spot for downloading .tgz files

2. Dealing with Google Takeout's Incomplete Files

Your observation is completely accurate: while Google is packaging massive multi-gigabyte files server-side, they appear in your Google Drive folder structure, but they are internally locked or incomplete. If your script fires midway through Google's upload cycle, it could download a broken, partial .tgz file and attempt to extract it, causing errors.

To address this, rclone has built-in features to handle this automatically.

Google Drive doesn't expose a partial file extension to third-party clients, but it does keep a rolling timestamp of when the file was last modified. Because of this, the bash script can be configured to use a safety boundary: ignore any file on Google Drive that has been modified or created within the last 24 hours.

Since Google Takeout operations usually complete within a few hours, a 24-hour buffer ensures your script only touches fully finalized, locked archives.

3. The Solidified, Secure Script Implementations

Here are the complete, production-ready versions of the pipeline scripts incorporating the clean folder layouts and safety boundaries.

The Shell Controller: ~/.photo_pipeline/run_takeout_pipeline.sh

#!/bin/bash

# Define strict absolute paths matching the hidden layout
PIPELINE_DIR="/Users/your_username/.photo_pipeline"
LOCAL_TEMP_DIR="$PIPELINE_DIR/takeout_staging"
PYTHON_SCRIPT_PATH="$PIPELINE_DIR/process_takeout.py"

echo "Checking Google Drive for completed archives..."
rclone copy gdrive:Home/Takeout "$LOCAL_TEMP_DIR" \
    --include "*.tgz" \
    --min-age 24h \
    --checksum \

    echo "Completed archives present. Initiating Python unpacker..."
    /usr/bin/python3 "$PYTHON_SCRIPT_PATH"
else

fi

echo "=== Pipeline Sync Finished ==="

FINAL_NAS_DIR = "/Volumes/YourNASVolume/Photos"

def process_tarball_archives():
    if not os.path.exists(CLOUD_SYNC_DIR):
        print(f"Directory missing: {CLOUD_SYNC_DIR}")
        return

    # Gather local .tgz items dropped by rclone
    archives = [f for f in os.listdir(CLOUD_SYNC_DIR) if f.endswith('.tgz')]
    
    if not archives:
        print("No localized archives to process.")
        return

    os.makedirs(EXTRACT_TEMP, exist_ok=True)

    for archive in sorted(archives):
        archive_path = os.path.join(CLOUD_SYNC_DIR, archive)
        print(f"\nExtracting archive file: {archive}")
        
        try:
            with tarfile.open(archive_path, "r:gz") as tar_ref:
                tar_ref.extractall(EXTRACT_TEMP)
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"✗ Extraction failed for {archive} (it might be corrupted): {e}")
            continue
            
        file_count = 0
        for root, _, files in os.walk(EXTRACT_TEMP):
            for file in files:
                if file.lower().endswith('.json') or file.startswith('.'):
                    continue
                    
                source_file = os.path.join(root, file)
                
                # Organize files chronologically by Current Year / Current Month
                target_folder = os.path.join(FINAL_NAS_DIR, datetime.now().strftime('%Y/%m'))
                os.makedirs(target_folder, exist_ok=True)
                
                dest_file = os.path.join(target_folder, file)
                
                # Check for file collisions
                if os.path.exists(dest_file):
                    name, ext = os.path.splitext(file)
                    dest_file = os.path.join(target_folder, f"{name}_{int(datetime.now().timestamp())}{ext}")
                    
                try:
                    shutil.move(source_file, dest_file)
                    file_count += 1
                except Exception as e:
                    print(f"  ✗ Failed to move file {file}: {e}")
                    
        # Reset local temporary staging directories
        shutil.rmtree(EXTRACT_TEMP)
        os.makedirs(EXTRACT_TEMP, exist_ok=True)
        
        # Safely delete the local archive copy so it doesn't process again
        os.remove(archive_path)
        print(f"✓ Integrated {file_count} media files from {archive} successfully.")

    if os.path.exists(EXTRACT_TEMP):
        shutil.rmtree(EXTRACT_TEMP)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    process_tarball_archives()
EOF

turns.response_html:
Ah, that's a classic Fish shell quirk! Fish doesn't handle the standard Bash-style << 'EOF' heredoc syntax the same way, which is why it's throwing that redirection error.

Since the script itself is written in Bash, the easiest way to bypass Fish's syntax restrictions is to drop into a temporary Bash shell, run the command, and then exit back to Fish.

Run this exact sequence in your terminal:

1. Drop into Bash

bash

2. Paste and Run the Block

Once your prompt changes to a Bash prompt, paste this entire block and hit enter:

cat << 'EOF' > ~/.photo_pipeline/run_takeout_pipeline.sh
#!/bin/bash

# Define strict absolute paths matching the layout
PIPELINE_DIR="$HOME/.photo_pipeline"
LOCAL_TEMP_DIR="$PIPELINE_DIR/takeout_staging"
PYTHON_SCRIPT_PATH="$PIPELINE_DIR/process_takeout.py"

echo "=== Pipeline Sync Started: $(date) ==="

# Sync only .tgz files older than 24 hours (protects against incomplete uploads)
echo "Checking Google Drive for completed archives..."
rclone copy gdrive:Home/Takeout "$LOCAL_TEMP_DIR" \
    --include "*.tgz" \
    --min-age 24h \
    --checksum \
    --progress

# Trigger processing only if files safely landed in staging
if [ -d "$LOCAL_TEMP_DIR" ] && [ "$(ls -A "$LOCAL_TEMP_DIR" | grep -v 'tmp_unpack')" ]; then
    echo "Completed archives present. Initiating Python unpacker..."
    /usr/bin/python3 "$PYTHON_SCRIPT_PATH"
else
    echo "No completely finalized archives found today. Exiting smoothly."
fi

echo "=== Pipeline Sync Finished ==="
EOF

chmod +x ~/.photo_pipeline/run_takeout_pipeline.sh

3. Return to Fish

Type exit and press enter to close the temporary Bash shell:

exit

Now the shell controller script is cleanly written and executable, and you are right back in your default Fish shell environment!

Once inside the Bash prompt, paste this complete updated code block:

cat << 'EOF' > ~/.photo_pipeline/process_takeout.py
# process_takeout.py
import os
import tarfile
import shutil
from datetime import datetime

# Paths
PIPELINE_DIR = os.path.expanduser("~/.photo_pipeline")
CLOUD_SYNC_DIR = os.path.join(PIPELINE_DIR, "takeout_staging")
EXTRACT_TEMP = os.path.join(CLOUD_SYNC_DIR, "tmp_unpack")
REPORT_PATH = os.path.join(PIPELINE_DIR, "report.md")

# Target NAS Destination (Adjust to match your exact NAS mount point volume)
FINAL_NAS_DIR = "/Volumes/YourNASVolume/Photos"

def process_tarball_archives():
    if not os.path.exists(CLOUD_SYNC_DIR):
        return

    archives = [f for f in os.listdir(CLOUD_SYNC_DIR) if f.endswith('.tgz')]
    
    if not archives:
        # Generate a status report even if nothing was found
        with open(REPORT_PATH, "w") as r:
            r.write(f"# 📸 Photo Ingest Pipeline Report\n")
            r.write(f"**Execution Timestamp:** {datetime.now().isoformat()}\n\n")
            r.write(f"## 📊 Summary\n* **Status:** IDLE\n* **Message:** No fresh archives were available in Google Drive staging today.\n")
        return

    os.makedirs(EXTRACT_TEMP, exist_ok=True)
    
    # Tracking for the report
    total_files = 0
    archive_details = []

    for archive in sorted(archives):
        archive_path = os.path.join(CLOUD_SYNC_DIR, archive)
        
        try:
            with tarfile.open(archive_path, "r:gz") as tar_ref:
                tar_ref.extractall(EXTRACT_TEMP)
        except Exception as e:
            archive_details.append(f"* `{archive}`: ✗ Failed extraction (corrupted archive). Error: {e}")
            continue
            
        file_count = 0
        for root, _, files in os.walk(EXTRACT_TEMP):
            for file in files:
                if file.lower().endswith('.json') or file.startswith('.'):
                    continue
                    
                source_file = os.path.join(root, file)
                target_folder = os.path.join(FINAL_NAS_DIR, datetime.now().strftime('%Y/%m'))
                os.makedirs(target_folder, exist_ok=True)
                
                dest_file = os.path.join(target_folder, file)
                
                if os.path.exists(dest_file):
                    name, ext = os.path.splitext(file)
                    dest_file = os.path.join(target_folder, f"{name}_{int(datetime.now().timestamp())}{ext}")
                    
                try:
                    shutil.move(source_file, dest_file)
                    file_count += 1
                except Exception:
                    pass
                    
        shutil.rmtree(EXTRACT_TEMP)
        os.makedirs(EXTRACT_TEMP, exist_ok=True)
        os.remove(archive_path)
        
        archive_details.append(f"* `{archive}`: Integrated {file_count} files.")
        total_files += file_count

    if os.path.exists(EXTRACT_TEMP):
        shutil.rmtree(EXTRACT_TEMP)

    # Write out the Markdown report file
    with open(REPORT_PATH, "w") as report:
        report.write(f"# 📸 Photo Ingest Pipeline Report\n")
        report.write(f"**Execution Timestamp:** {datetime.now().isoformat()}\n\n")
        report.write(f"## 📊 Summary\n")
        report.write(f"* **Status:** SUCCESS\n")
        report.write(f"* **Archives Processed:** {len(archives)}\n")
        report.write(f"* **Total Media Assets Integrated:** {total_files} files\n\n")
        report.write(f"## 📦 Detailed Archive Breakdown\n")
        for detail in archive_details:
            report.write(f"{detail}\n")
        report.write(f"\n---\n*Report generated automatically by com.user.photo_sync*\n")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    process_tarball_archives()
EOF
